articles.title: How the Champions League Actually Works Now
articles.seoTitle: Champions League Format Explained: The 36-Team League Phase
articles.excerpt: The group stage is gone. One 36-team table, eight matches against eight different opponents, and a bottom twelve who go home with nothing. Here is the format, and what it changed.
articles.author: Ibrahim Sodiq
articles.metaDescription: A clear explainer of the Champions League league-phase format: 36 teams, eight opponents, the top-eight bye, the play-off round and the seeding that shapes the bracket.

content.heading: One table, not eight groups
content.body:
From the 2024–25 season the Champions League abandoned the group stage it had used for three decades. Instead of eight groups of four, all 36 clubs now sit in a single league table.

The number of participants rose from 32 to 36. Each club plays eight matches — four at home, four away — against eight different opponents, and never plays the same team twice. Points work exactly as they do in a domestic league: three for a win, one for a draw.

The format is drawn from the Swiss system used in chess tournaments, where players are matched by strength rather than sorted into fixed pools. For the draw, the 36 clubs are divided into four seeding pots by UEFA club coefficient, and each team is drawn against two opponents from each pot, playing one home and one away in each pairing.

The league phase runs from September to January. The knockout rounds begin in February.

content.heading: What the table decides
content.body:
When the eight matches are done, the single table splits three ways.

Positions 1 to 8 go straight into the round of 16. They skip February entirely and enter the draw as seeded teams.

Positions 9 to 24 enter a two-legged knockout play-off round in February — eight ties for the remaining eight places in the last 16. Teams finishing 9th to 16th are seeded in that draw; teams finishing 17th to 24th are not.

Positions 25 to 36 are eliminated. This is the change that most altered the competition's stakes: under the previous format, third place in a group meant a drop into the Europa League. Now the bottom twelve are out of European football for the season, with no parachute.

Finishing ninth and finishing twenty-fourth both mean the play-off round, but they are not the same outcome. The seeding advantage runs all the way through the bracket.

content.heading: Why league position still matters after the league phase
content.body:
The knockout bracket is shaped by where you finished, and the advantage compounds.

Higher-ranked sides get the second leg at home — in the play-off round for those seeded 9th to 16th, and in the round of 16 for the top eight. The top four in the league phase carry that advantage into the quarter-finals, and the top two into the semi-finals.

The top eight are also paired in the draw so that the sides finishing first and second land on opposite sides of the bracket, meaning the two best league-phase records cannot meet before the final.

One useful wrinkle: if an unseeded club knocks out a seeded one, it inherits that seeding position for the rest of the run. The bracket keeps its shape even when the favourites do not survive it.

content.heading: Getting in: the qualifying rounds nobody watches
content.body:
The 36 clubs in the league phase do not all arrive the same way, and most of the field is settled long before September.

Twenty-nine teams qualify in advance: the Champions League and Europa League title holders, the champions of the ten highest-ranked associations, runners-up from the top six, third-placed teams from the top five, fourth-placed teams from the top four, and two places awarded to the associations with the best one-year coefficient.

The remaining seven come through qualifying, which begins in early July — before most domestic seasons have even started. Qualifying is split into two separate streams: a Champions Path for teams that won their national league, and a League Path for those who qualified by finishing second, third or fourth. Five of the seven places go to the Champions Path and two to the League Path.

That split is deliberate. It protects a route into the competition for champions of smaller associations, who would otherwise be drawn against clubs from far stronger leagues at every stage.

content.heading: What the format changed in practice
content.body:
Three things are measurably different.

More matches. Guaranteed group-stage football went from six matches to eight. A club reaching the final can now play up to 17 matches in the competition, against a previous maximum of 13.

More variety of opponent. Eight different opponents rather than three played twice means a wider spread of fixtures, and it removes the dead rubber — the final group game between two teams who had already settled their fate.

Harsher elimination. Finishing outside the top 24 ends your European season outright.

The honest caveat: whether the format is better is an argument about taste and calendar congestion, not a question with a factual answer. What is not in dispute is that clubs now need deeper squads. Eight matches against eight different opponents inside ten weeks cannot be navigated with the small core that a four-team group allowed.

articles.title: Champions League Records: Who Actually Holds What
articles.seoTitle: Champions League Records: Most Titles, Most Finals Lost, Every Multiple Winner
articles.excerpt: Real Madrid's fifteen, the five-in-a-row nobody has matched, Juventus's seven lost finals, and the four clubs who reached a final in their own stadium. The records, with the awkward ones included.
articles.author: Ibrahim Sodiq
articles.metaDescription: Champions League and European Cup records: most titles, consecutive wins, most finals lost, the multiple-winner badge, and the clubs who lost finals in their own stadium.

content.heading: The competition, briefly
content.body:
The competition was established in 1955 and was called the European Cup until it was renamed ahead of the 1992–93 season. Every record below spans both eras, because they are the same trophy and the same lineage.

In seventy years, 24 clubs have won it.

content.heading: Most titles: Real Madrid, and it is not close
content.body:
Real Madrid hold fifteen titles, including the very first edition in 1956.

They also hold the record for consecutive wins, with five straight titles from 1956 to 1960 — a run that has never been approached since, and which the current format makes structurally harder to repeat.

By country, Spain has produced the most champions with twenty wins from just two clubs. England has fifteen wins from a record six different clubs — the widest spread of any nation. Italy has twelve from three.

That English figure comes with an asterisk that is part of the record: English clubs were banned from European competition for five years after the Heysel disaster in 1985.

content.heading: The multiple-winner badge
content.body:
A club that wins the competition three times in a row, or five times in total, earns the multiple-winner badge worn on the shirt in European competition.

Six clubs have earned it: Real Madrid, Ajax, Bayern Munich, AC Milan, Liverpool and Barcelona.

There used to be a second prize attached. Until 2009, a club reaching that threshold was allowed to keep the European Champion Clubs' Cup itself, and UEFA commissioned a new one. Since 2009 the winners each year receive a full-size replica and UEFA retains the original trophy.

content.heading: The records nobody wants
content.body:
Juventus have lost seven finals — more than any other club.

Atlético Madrid are the only side to have reached three finals without ever winning the trophy. Reims, Valencia and Arsenal have each finished runners-up twice without winning it.

And then there is the cruellest category in the competition's history. The venue for the final is chosen years in advance, and on four occasions a club has reached a final scheduled for its own stadium.

Two of them took the chance. Real Madrid won their second European Cup at the Santiago Bernabéu in 1957, and Inter Milan won their second at the San Siro in 1965.

The other two lost — both on penalties. Roma were beaten by Liverpool at the Stadio Olimpico in 1984, and Bayern Munich were beaten by Chelsea at the Allianz Arena in 2012.

content.heading: The current holders
content.body:
Paris Saint-Germain are the reigning champions, having won the 2026 final 4–3 on penalties against Arsenal after a 1–1 draw following extra time.

It is PSG's second title. For Arsenal it was a second final lost without a win — which is how they join Reims and Valencia in the runners-up column above.

content.heading: A note on how these records are counted
content.body:
Records in this competition are usually quoted for the combined European Cup and Champions League era, which is why Real Madrid's total includes titles from the 1950s and why Ajax's badge rests substantially on the early 1970s.

Appearance and goalscoring records are counted differently by different sources depending on whether qualifying rounds are included, so they are deliberately left out here rather than quoted with a caveat that most readers will not notice. The club records above are drawn from the finals record itself, where the count is unambiguous.

articles.title: Premier League 2026/27: Every Confirmed Date Before Kick-Off
articles.seoTitle: Premier League 2026/27 Start Date, Opening Fixtures & Key Dates
articles.excerpt: Arsenal host Coventry City on Friday 21 August to open the season. Here is the full opening round, who came up, who came down, the managers who changed and every confirmed date — no predictions.
articles.author: Ibrahim Sodiq
articles.metaDescription: When the 2026/27 Premier League season starts, the full opening-weekend fixture list with kick-off times and broadcasters, promoted and relegated clubs, managerial changes and every confirmed date.

content.heading: When it starts
content.body:
The 2026/27 Premier League season begins on Friday 21 August 2026, when champions Arsenal host newly promoted Coventry City at the Emirates Stadium. Kick-off is 20:00 BST, live on Sky Sports.

The season ends on Sunday 30 May 2027, when all ten final-round fixtures kick off simultaneously, as they do every year.

Both dates are later than a normal Premier League season, and there is a specific reason for that.

content.heading: Why the season starts so late this year
content.body:
The 2026 World Cup pushed everything back. The Premier League's opening match falls 34 days after the World Cup final in the United States.

That compression shows up in the structure of the season rather than in the number of games. There are still 380 matches and 38 rounds, but they are arranged as 33 weekend rounds and five midweek rounds. The Premier League has said the schedule is designed to avoid clashes with UEFA competition dates wherever possible.

The fixture list itself was released on 19 June 2026.

content.heading: The full opening round
content.body:
The first match round is spread across four days, from Friday 21 to Monday 24 August. All times BST.

Friday 21 August — Arsenal v Coventry City, 20:00, Sky Sports.

Saturday 22 August — Hull City v Manchester United, 12:30, TNT Sports. Everton v Crystal Palace, 15:00. Ipswich Town v Sunderland, 15:00. Nottingham Forest v Leeds United, 15:00. Brentford v Tottenham Hotspur, 17:30, Sky Sports.

Sunday 23 August — Brighton & Hove Albion v Aston Villa, 14:00, Sky Sports. Manchester City v AFC Bournemouth, 14:00, Sky Sports. Newcastle United v Liverpool, 16:30, Sky Sports.

Monday 24 August — Fulham v Chelsea, 20:00, Sky Sports.

Kick-off times later in the season are routinely moved for television and for clubs' progress in European and domestic cups, so treat anything beyond the opening rounds as provisional until it is confirmed.

content.heading: Who came up, who went down
content.body:
Three clubs were promoted from the Championship. Coventry City went up as champions under Frank Lampard, and their opening fixture at Arsenal is their first top-flight match in 25 years. Ipswich Town took the second automatic place. Hull City completed the line-up by winning the play-off final against Middlesbrough.

They replace West Ham United, Burnley and Wolverhampton Wanderers, all relegated at the end of 2025/26.

The defending champions are Arsenal, who won their first Premier League title since 2004 under Mikel Arteta.

content.heading: The managers who changed
content.body:
Three of the biggest jobs in the league changed hands over the summer, and all three new managers take charge of a competitive Premier League fixture for the first time on the opening weekend.

Andoni Iraola replaced Arne Slot at Liverpool, and his first league match is away at Newcastle United on the Sunday. Xabi Alonso is the new manager at Chelsea, starting with a trip across London to Fulham on the Monday night. Enzo Maresca replaced Pep Guardiola at Manchester City, beginning at home to Bournemouth.

The full club-by-club picture of who changed and who stayed is on our managers page for the season.

content.heading: Every other confirmed date
content.body:
Transfer windows. The summer window closes on Tuesday 1 September 2026 at 11pm UK time. The winter window opens on Friday 1 January 2027 and closes on Monday 1 February 2027 at 11pm.

International breaks. 21 September to 6 October 2026, 9 to 17 November 2026, and 22 to 30 March 2027.

Europe. The Champions League league-phase draw is on Thursday 27 August 2026, with the league phase beginning 8 to 10 September. The Champions League final is on Saturday 5 June 2027, the week after the Premier League's final day.

Domestic cups. Premier League clubs not in European competition enter the Carabao Cup in the second round, in the week commencing 24 August; the rest enter in the third round in September. The Carabao Cup final is on Sunday 21 March 2027 at Wembley. The FA Cup third round, where Premier League clubs enter, is on 9 January 2027.

Before any of it, the Community Shield between Arsenal and Manchester City was scheduled for Sunday 16 August 2026 at the Principality Stadium in Cardiff.

content.heading: Television
content.body:
Sky Sports will show a minimum of 215 live Premier League matches in 2026/27. TNT Sports holds a separate package, which includes Hull City v Manchester United on the opening Saturday.

Six of the ten opening-round fixtures are on Sky Sports.

content.heading: What this page will not do
content.body:
There are no predictions here, no projected table and no tip about who goes down. Every line above is a confirmed date, a confirmed fixture or a completed transaction, and each one is checked against the sources listed below.

BRYME's match pages fill in results, lineups and statistics only after a match has actually been played. Before kick-off they carry the fixture details and nothing that pretends to be analysis of a game nobody has seen.

If a kick-off time on this page differs from what you see elsewhere later in the season, the broadcaster selections have moved it. Check the official fixture list rather than this page.

articles.title: Arsenal 3-0 Manchester City: Maresca's First Day Went About as Badly as It Could
articles.seoTitle: Arsenal 3-0 Manchester City: 2026 Community Shield Report & Goals
articles.excerpt: Arsenal led inside the opening minute and were three up two minutes into the second half. Enzo Maresca's first competitive match as Manchester City manager finished with Arsenal fans singing at him.
articles.author: Ibrahim Sodiq
articles.metaDescription: Arsenal beat Manchester City 3-0 in the 2026 FA Community Shield at the Principality Stadium. Calafiori, Havertz and Odegaard scored in Enzo Maresca's first competitive match in charge of City.

content.heading: The result
content.body:
Arsenal beat Manchester City 3-0 at the Principality Stadium in Cardiff on Sunday 16 August 2026 to win the FA Community Shield.

Riccardo Calafiori scored inside the opening minute, finishing after being played in by Myles Lewis-Skelly. Kai Havertz made it two on 28 minutes from a Christos Tzolis delivery. Martin Odegaard added the third two minutes into the second half, again set up by Tzolis, taking the ball round Gianluigi Donnarumma before finishing.

Samuel Barrott refereed. Odegaard, as captain, lifted the trophy.

content.heading: Twenty-three seconds
content.body:
The opening goal arrived before Manchester City had settled into the match — timed at 23 seconds by The Athletic, 24 by several other outlets. Either way, it is the first goal scored in the opening minute of a Community Shield since Bobby Owen did it for Manchester City against West Bromwich Albion in 1968.

That is the sort of statistic that usually decorates a report. Here it framed the whole afternoon. City spent the rest of the game chasing a match that had been shaped before they touched the ball properly, and they never really got hold of it. David Raya's most demanding moment did not arrive until Rayan Cherki tested him from range in the second half.

Arsenal's 3-0 is the biggest winning margin in a Community Shield since 2014 — when Arsenal beat Manchester City by the same score under Arsène Wenger.

content.heading: Maresca's first competitive match
content.body:
This was Enzo Maresca's first competitive fixture since replacing Pep Guardiola, and the first real look at Manchester City in the post-Guardiola era. It could hardly have gone worse. By the second half, Arsenal supporters were directing chants of “you're getting sacked in the morning” at him.

A Community Shield is, as TNT Sports pundit Joleon Lescott noted, effectively a pre-season game. His concern was the margin rather than the defeat: “the gap between the two sides in this particular encounter is probably as big as any gap between the sides I've seen in a long, long time.”

There were mitigating details. Erling Haaland had only recently returned to training after the World Cup and was withdrawn on 53 minutes. Several City players are short of match sharpness for the same reason. And Maresca's own response pointed at the squad rather than the performance — he said the sooner City can make signings, the better.

Ruben Dias, who captained the side, was blunter, telling TNT Sports: “It's the beginning of the season but it's not good enough.”

Donnarumma's afternoon will attract attention too. He fumbled the ball in the build-up to Arsenal's second and was comprehensively beaten by Odegaard for the third.

content.heading: What it says about Arsenal, carefully
content.body:
Mikel Arteta said the performance must set the “standard” for the season. That is a manager's framing, and it is worth keeping some distance from it.

What is factual: the reigning Premier League champions beat the FA Cup holders comprehensively, scored three, conceded none, and were still attacking at 3-0 rather than protecting the lead — Bukayo Saka came close to a fourth late on. Arsenal have now won four Community Shields in the last ten years.

What is not factual is anything about how the title race will go. This was one match in August between two teams at different stages of their pre-season, one of which has just lost the most successful manager in its history. A Community Shield has predicted very little historically, and this site is not going to pretend otherwise five days before the league starts.

content.heading: What happens next
content.body:
Arsenal begin their title defence on Friday 21 August at home to newly promoted Coventry City, the opening fixture of the 2026/27 Premier League season, kicking off at 20:00 BST.

Manchester City start on Sunday 23 August at home to AFC Bournemouth at 14:00 — Maresca's first Premier League match in charge.

Our full guide to the 2026/27 season, with every confirmed date and the complete opening round, is linked below.

content.heading: A note on this report
content.body:
The Community Shield is not a Premier League fixture, so it does not appear in BRYME's match centre, which covers the five domestic leagues we track. The score, scorers, timings, referee and quotes above were checked against the sources listed below before publication.

Where sources disagreed — on whether Calafiori's goal came at 23 or 24 seconds — both figures are given rather than one being picked.

articles.title: English Champions Since 1888: How the Title Was Won, and by Whom
articles.seoTitle: English Football Champions Since 1888: Full History and Title Counts
articles.excerpt: Preston won the first one without losing a game. Twenty-four clubs have won it since. The story of the English title is really the story of four structural changes — and who benefited from each.
articles.author: Ibrahim Sodiq
articles.metaDescription: The history of the English football championship from 1888: Preston's unbeaten first title, the 1892 split into two divisions, the 1961 abolition of the maximum wage, the 1992 Premier League breakaway, and every club to have won it.

content.heading: It starts with a meeting, not a match
content.body:
The Football Association codified professional football in 1885. Three years later the Football League was established, after meetings initiated by William McGregor, a director of Aston Villa.

That is the actual origin of the English championship: not a grand founding vision but an administrator solving a scheduling problem for clubs who had just been allowed to pay their players and needed guaranteed fixtures to afford it.

The first season was 1888–89.

content.heading: Preston won the first one without losing
content.body:
Preston North End were the first English champions, and they completed their league fixtures unbeaten.

It is worth pausing on how rarely that has been matched in the 130-odd seasons since. Preston did it in the very first attempt, in a competition of twelve clubs, and it remains one of the few genuinely unrepeatable achievements in the sport — not because the football was harder, but because a twelve-team league no longer exists to be won that way.

content.heading: The league was a northern competition first
content.body:
For its first four seasons the Football League contained only twelve to fourteen clubs, and every one of them came from the North of England or the Midlands.

This was not a quirk of geography. Professionalism had been embraced more readily in the North and the Midlands than in the South, where the amateur tradition held on longer. The southern clubs that now dominate the English game were, at the point the championship was invented, not part of it at all.

The league expanded in 1892 by absorbing its rival, the Football Alliance. With 28 members it split into two divisions: most former Alliance clubs went into the new Second Division, the original league became the First Division, and promotion and relegation between them began.

That structure — a top division you can be thrown out of — is now so fundamental to English football that it is easy to forget it was an administrative consequence of a merger.

content.heading: Two changes that moved the money
content.body:
The two developments that most shaped who wins the title were financial, not sporting.

In 1961 the rules imposing a maximum wage on players were abolished. The effect was immediate and structural: power shifted towards the bigger clubs, because for the first time they could convert greater revenue directly into better players. Before 1961 a wealthy club could not simply outbid a poorer one for a footballer's signature. After it, they could.

In 1992 the clubs then in the First Division defected to form the FA Premier League, which became the new top tier. A series of progressively larger television contracts has since put unprecedented wealth into the hands of top-flight clubs.

Both changes did the same thing in different eras: they widened the gap between what the richest clubs could spend and what everyone else could. Every debate about competitive balance in English football traces back to one or both.

content.heading: Who has actually won it
content.body:
Twenty-four clubs have been English champions.

Liverpool and Manchester United share the record with 20 titles each.

The current champions are Arsenal, who won the 2025–26 title — their 14th English championship.

The spread matters as much as the top of the list. Twenty-four different winners across more than a century sounds competitive, and in the early decades it was; the concentration is a recent phenomenon, and it lines up closely with the two financial changes above rather than with anything that happened on a pitch.

content.heading: A note on counting
content.body:
Title counts in English football combine three competitions that are really one lineage: the Football League from 1888 to 1892, the Football League First Division from 1892 to 1992, and the Premier League from 1992 onwards.

This is why you will sometimes see two different numbers quoted for the same club — one counting all English championships, the other counting only Premier League titles since 1992. Neither is wrong; they answer different questions. Every figure on this page is the full count across all three eras, which is the standard used in the official record.
